chapters.title: Chapter 3: Cointegration — Testing Whether a Pair Really Mean-Reverts

lessons.title: Correlation vs Cointegration: Why They Are Not the Same Thing

children.text: A trader builds a stat arb model on two large Nifty IT stocks. Over five years, their daily returns show a correlation of about 0.85, consistently, year after year. He treats this as strong evidence the pair is tradeable, builds a position betting their price ratio will revert to its historical average, and holds through what he assumes is just a temporary stretch. Eighteen months later, the position is down sharply. The price ratio never reverted. It kept drifting in the same direction the entire time, even as the daily return correlation stayed just as high as before. Correlation told him the truth about how the stocks moved day to day. It told him nothing about whether their price levels would ever come back together, which turned out to be the only question that actually mattered for his trade.

body.text: Correlation measures how two stocks' short-term returns move together. Cointegration measures something different and stronger: whether a specific combination of their price levels has a stable, self-correcting long-run relationship. A pair can have one property without the other, and a stat arb trade specifically needs the second one.

columns.label: Correlation
points: Asks: do the two returns move together, day to day?
A short-run, backward-looking measure of co-movement
Says nothing about whether price levels ever converge

columns.label: Cointegration
points: Asks: does a specific combination of the two price levels revert to a stable mean?
Computed on price levels, via the regression residual spread
A long-run, structural measure of a genuine equilibrium relationship
The actual property a stat arb trade needs in order to work

children.text: How a Pair Can Be Correlated but Not Cointegrated

Take two large Nifty IT majors like TCS and Infosys. Both report revenue overwhelmingly in US dollars, both are exposed to the same rupee-dollar rate, the same US client budget cycles, and the same broad IT services sentiment. Their daily returns move together closely for exactly these shared reasons, which is why their return correlation tends to stay high and fairly stable. None of that requires their price levels to stay anchored to each other. If one company's deal wins and margin profile structurally improve relative to the other over several years, its valuation can re-rate permanently higher, and their price ratio can drift steadily in one direction for years, all while daily returns keep moving together just as closely as before.

body.text: This is the exact opposite of what a stat arb trader actually needs. High, stable correlation reassures you the two stocks are moving for the same underlying reasons. It tells you nothing about whether the gap between their price levels, the actual spread you would trade, ever closes. In this illustrative example, it never does.

children.text: How a Pair Can Be Cointegrated With Only Moderate Correlation

The reverse can also be true. Lesson 8's Britannia Industries and Nestle India case study found a return correlation of only about 0.60, moderate at best, largely because the two companies have meaningfully different product mixes and don't react identically to every piece of category-specific news. That does not rule out cointegration. What actually determines cointegration is whether some real, ongoing structural force keeps their relative valuation anchored over the long run. Both being large, comparably positioned FMCG staples held by much the same set of long-only domestic and foreign investors is exactly that kind of anchor, whether or not their day-to-day returns track each other closely.

An even sharper real-world example is a listed holding company and the operating businesses it holds stakes in, the kind of structure seen with groups like Bajaj Holdings & Investment holding stakes in Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv. The holding company's fair value is mechanically tied to the market value of what it owns. That mechanical link can keep the holding company's price anchored to its subsidiaries' combined value over the long run, a genuine cointegrating relationship, even though day-to-day return correlation between the holding company and any one subsidiary might be unremarkable, since the holding company also reflects the other stakes it holds.

A property of two or more non-stationary price series where a specific weighted combination of them is stationary, meaning it has a stable mean and reverts to it.

body.label: What actually needs to be tested before trading a pair
body.context: Not just the correlation of returns. A high correlation reading alone has never been sufficient evidence that a pair is tradeable.

body.title: Correlated, but is it cointegrated?
body.question: Two stocks show a 0.9 return correlation over three years. Over the same period, their price ratio has trended steadily upward with no sign of reverting. What is the most accurate conclusion?
options: The two stocks are both correlated and cointegrated
The two stocks are correlated, but there is no evidence here that they are cointegrated
A correlation of 0.9 proves cointegration on its own
Cointegration does not matter if correlation is high enough
body.explanation: High correlation describes how returns move together day to day. It says nothing about whether price levels have a self-correcting long-run relationship. A price ratio that trends without reverting is direct evidence against cointegration, regardless of how high the return correlation is.

body.title: What would change your mind?
body.scenario: You are looking at two auto ancillary stocks. Their return correlation is a modest 0.55. A colleague dismisses the pair immediately: "too low, not worth testing further."
body.prompt: Is he right to dismiss it purely on correlation? What would you want to check before agreeing with him?
body.modelAnswer: Not necessarily. A moderate correlation does not rule out cointegration, especially if there is a real structural reason the two companies' valuations should stay anchored together, shared customers, shared input costs, or a similar ownership base. Rather than dismissing the pair on correlation alone, you would want to build the regression-based spread and formally test it for stationarity (Lessons 10 and 11) before deciding either way.

cards.definition: A property of two or more non-stationary price series where a specific weighted combination of them is stationary, meaning it has a stable mean and reverts to it. The actual property a stat arb trade needs.
A series with a stable mean and variance over time, that reverts to its own average rather than wandering off. Covered formally as a testable property in Lesson 10.
A series, like most individual stock prices, whose level wanders over time with no fixed point it reverts to. Also described as having a unit root.

A real, ongoing economic or ownership link between two securities, such as shared fundamentals or a holding company's stake in a subsidiary, that can keep their relative valuation cointegrated over the long run.

points: Correlation measures how two stocks' returns move together day to day. Cointegration measures whether a specific combination of their price levels reverts to a stable, long-run mean. These are different properties.
A pair can show high, stable return correlation for years while their price levels drift apart permanently, with no reversion. High correlation alone is not evidence of cointegration.

A pair can be cointegrated with only moderate return correlation, if a real structural anchor, shared fundamentals, similar investor base, or an ownership link, keeps their relative valuation anchored over the long run.

The property a stat arb trade actually needs is that the regression residual spread from Chapter 2 is stationary. Lessons 10 and 11 cover how to test for this formally, rather than assuming it from a correlation reading.
Correlated and cointegrated together is the strongest, most typical stat arb candidate. Either one alone is not enough.

The TCS/Infosys scenario and all correlation and price-ratio figures used here are illustrative and hypothetical, not actual historical data. The reference to Bajaj Holdings & Investment's stakes in Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv reflects a real, publicly known group structure, used only to illustrate the type of structural anchor described, not as a claim about actual historical cointegration or price behavior between these entities.
